On 13 November 2026, the Norwegian Supreme Court, sitting as an eleven-judge Grand Chamber, delivered a landmark judgment in the North Sea Fields case. The Court held that environmental impact assessments (EIAs) must address downstream emissions from burning extracted oil and gas (Scope 3). By a 6–5 majority, it also required the emissions of Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil to be assessed alongside those of other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. Finding that the Ministry of Energy had failed to meet this requirement, even in its subsequent assessments, the Court declared the development approvals invalid (HR-2026-2428-S, paras 225, 234, 244), short of ordering operations to stop. The decision’s constitutional significance lies in the role of procedural environmental rights, which ultimately require thorough and independent assessments, as well as the inclusive participation of the public in how the State assesses climate harm.
Greenpeace Nordic and Natur og Ungdom (Nature and Youth) brought the proceedings against the Norwegian State. Save the Children Norway intervened through written submissions on children’s rights. The Norwegian Association of Local and Regional Authorities and the Norwegian National Human Rights Institution also submitted observations.
The three developments hold an estimated 875 million barrels of oil equivalent. Yet, the ruling matters beyond this scale: it challenges the assessment of petroleum projects in isolation.
The Road to the Supreme Court
In June 2023, the environmental organisations challenged the approvals of the three Plans for Development and Operation (PDOs), arguing that the EIAs had omitted emissions from the eventual combustion of the oil and gas. They also sought interim relief.
In January 2024, the Oslo District Court declared the approvals invalid and granted interim relief. In the appeals brought by the State, the Borgarting Court of Appeal suspended the injunction and sought an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court, which held in May 2025 that the EIA Directive required downstream combustion emissions to be assessed (Case E-18/24).
Meanwhile, the operators submitted supplementary environmental reports, followed by public consultations. In August and December 2024, the Ministry decided not to revoke the approvals. In November 2025, the Court of Appeal declared those decisions invalid: although it considered the supplementary reports sufficient, the Ministry’s own assessment was deemed deficient, and the State appealed.
While the appeal was pending, the government in May 2026 issued a Royal Decree declining to revoke the approvals, but the appeal decided by the Supreme Court concerned only the Ministry’s 2024 decisions.
This Norwegian case has already travelled. The Oslo District Court judgment was cited by the UK Supreme Court in Finch v Surrey County Council ([2024] UKSC 20, paras 169–172). Finch, in turn, was later relied upon by the Scottish Court of Session in quashing the Jackdaw and Rosebank consents (Greenpeace Ltd v Advocate General for Scotland, [2025] CSOH 10). Meanwhile, in Norway, the Borgarting Court of Appeal referred questions concerning downstream emissions to the EFTA Court (Case E-18/24), whose advisory opinion was cited by Judges Bhandari and Cleveland in their joint declaration attached to the ICJ’s Advisory Opinion on Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change (Joint declaration, para 16 with reference to Case E-18/24, para 17), as well as by the Danish Energy Board of Appeals, which required reconsideration for the approval of the Hejre oil field.
The Supreme Court’s Decision
At first glance, the judgment turns on whether Article 3(1) of the EU EIA Directive (2011/92/EU) encompasses downstream combustion emissions among a project’s significant direct and indirect effects. But its reasoning reaches further, engaging with causation, cumulative harm and the constitutional value of environmental procedure, and is historic in both breadth and depth.
In breadth, the majority, led by Justice Poulsen, situated the Directive within a wider legal landscape. It referred to the ICJ’s view that customary international law requires States to exercise due diligence to prevent significant climate harm and to consider cumulative effects of activities under their jurisdiction or control (paras 177). The Court also drew on the ECtHR’s Greenpeace Nordic v Norway, under which authorities must consider whether petroleum developments are compatible with national and international obligations to protect against climate harm (paras 184–191).
In depth, the decision is anchored in consequential reasoning. Once extracted, oil and gas will almost inevitably be burned, generating emissions unless carbon capture intervenes (paras 149–150). This reasoning can be called the logical inseparability of extraction and combustion, and it reflects IPCC science, whose findings Norway had already recognised, alongside its domestic and international climate commitments (paras 99–107, 151).
According to the Court, the EIA Directive’s requirement that gross combustion emissions be not only described, but also assessed in an EIA before approval of a PDO is consistent with the wording of Norway’s Petroleum Act and the Petroleum Regulations, and could be gleaned already from the first climate case against the Norwegian state, Peoples v Arctic Oil, which was decided in 2020, whereby “global climate effects” are to be subject to an EIA in connection with an application for PDO approval (HR-2020-2472-P, paras 212, 214, 216, 218 and 241 as cited in para 155).
Further, the court held that neither the EIA Directive nor international and regional law impose a more extensive obligation to carry out an EIA in proceedings concerning PDO approval that also considers the global climate budget or consequential effects. On the global carbon budget, the court referred to the Paris Agreement Article 4 (as referenced in para 189) and Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) on the obligation to carry out “adequate, timely and comprehensive” EIAs (People v Arctic Oil, para 318, as quoted in para 184).   Similarly, when describing the project’s “direct effects and any indirect, secondary and cumulative effects”, the EIA Directive does not impose the carbon budget approach as account should, rather than shall, be taken of “the environmental protection objectives established at Union or Member State level which are relevant to the project”(point 5, para 2, of Annex IV to the EIA Directive, as referenced in paras 181 and 182). In contrast, the Court of Appeal had held that assessments were to be carried out in light of the remaining global carbon budgets, that is, the maximum amount of CO₂ that can be released into the atmosphere before the temperature rises to a given level (para 179).
On consequential effects, the Norwegian Supreme Court stated that there is no doubt that an EIA must cover the project’s effects on all the factors listed in Article 3(1) of the EIA Directive, namely human beings, human health, biodiversity, land, soil, water, air, climate, material assets, cultural heritage and landscape, as well as the interactions between these factors (para 194). The Court clarified, however, that the question at issue was a different one: whether the assessment must also encompass the consequential effects that the project’s impacts on one or more of these factors may have on other factors, and answered in the negative (paras 196ff).
The Norwegian Continental Shelf, and Its Dissent
The disagreement between the majority and minority judges concerned cumulative assessment. The majority holds that the EIA Directive requires an impact assessment to describe and assess the combustion emissions both of the project at hand and, cumulatively, of other existing and approved projects on the Norwegian shelf, together with their effect on global temperature rise (paras 178 and 214ff). The State argued that cumulation matters only to prevent “salami-slicing”, that is, splitting a project to dodge the assessment threshold. The majority rejected this: cumulation governs not only whether an assessment is triggered, but also what it must contain (paras 164–165). Two limits frame this duty: the continental shelf, because Norway can license petroleum nowhere else (para 167) and the petroleum sector, since adding every other sector would make the assessment disproportionately burdensome (para 168). The majority also stressed that the duty can be easily fulfilled by reference to reserve data for every field, which is public, and simple computations on gross emissions and their warming effect (para 176). Therefore, in light of Articles 3 and 8 of the EIA Directive and the relevant Norwegian implementing legislation, the authorities must carry out an independent assessment of the effects described in the EIA report. Furthermore, the authorities must assess whether conditions should be imposed with a view to limiting and mitigating significant adverse effects (paras 219 ff).
The dissent, penned by Justice Sivertsen, did not challenge the inclusion of downstream combustion emissions within the EIA Directive. Rather, it disputed the majority’s extension of the assessment to cumulative emissions from other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. For the dissenting justices, an assessment of each project’s gross combustion emissions and their climate effects was sufficient. Accordingly, they found no grounds for invalidating the Ministry’s 2024 decisions (paras 260–264).
The narrow 6–5 majority in the 2026 judgment invites comparison with the Norwegian Supreme Court’s first climate ruling in 2020, when the Court upheld the contested petroleum licences by 11 votes to four. While the outcome differed, there is a striking pattern of judicial continuity.
Seven judges participated in both decisions. Three of the four dissenting judges in 2020 – Webster, Falch and Østensen Berglund – joined the majority in 2026. Conversely, three members of the 2020 majority – Falkanger, Høgetveit Berg and Steinsvik – joined the 2026 dissent. Chief Justice Øie sided with the majority in both cases.
This alignment is particularly interesting because the 2020 dissent was already concerned with the adequacy of EIAs and the need for meaningful judicial scrutiny of procedural requirements. Justice Webster, writing for the minority, argued that judicial restraint in reviewing the substantive environmental choices of the political branches made effective scrutiny of the decision-making procedure all the more important (HR-2020-2472-P, para. 256).
Although the two judgments concern different stages of petroleum authorisation, different legal questions, and an evolving legal framework, the voting patterns suggest a degree of continuity in individual judicial approaches to environmental assessment, institutional deference and the consequences of procedural shortcomings. This observation resonates with Jørn Øyrehagen Sunde’s historical account of the Norwegian Supreme Court. Øyrehagen Sunde connects the Court’s increasingly active role in judicial review with broader institutional developments and internationalisation. In particular, he describes the growing role of legal norms originating beyond Norway’s borders in plenary and Grand Chamber decisions. Viewed through a judicial politics perspective, the 2026 judgment therefore raises a question extending beyond the immediate dispute: How does the internationalisation of law reshape the balance between judicial restraint and effective scrutiny of executive decision-making?
Procedural review, in this sense, is neither procedural formalism nor procedural fetishism. What appears as a procedural turn in climate adjudication may reflect a deeper institutional transformation. The internationalisation of legal norms, instead of allowing courts to “make” climate policy, has empowered their capacity – and responsibility – to scrutinise the legal conditions under which such policy is implemented.
Constitutional Rights and Effective Judicial Review
EIA obligations must be understood in light of Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution, as recognised in the first Norwegian climate case (HR-2020-2472-P, paras 182–183, as cited in para 221). As the majority writes, “[f]or judicial review to be effective, it is essential that reasons be given”, clearly demonstrating that combustion emissions and their effects on global temperature rise have been taken into account and assessed (para 222).
The royal decree passed by the Norwegian government in May 2026, which reassessed the petroleum approvals, offered a more detailed justification than its 2024 decisions, including an assessment of the emissions’ contribution to climate change. Yet, it still failed to consider the cumulative combustion emissions from existing and approved petroleum fields on the Norwegian continental shelf. Even more importantly, the cumulative climate impacts also should have been addressed in the developers’ environmental impact reports and subjected to public consultation (paras 233–234).
The majority then explains why such an omission invalidates the decisions. Rules on impact assessment for interventions in nature are procedural rules to be enforced strictly, in light of Section 112 of the Constitution and the intensive review it calls for. Their purpose is not only to identify the political trade-offs for the authorities. It is also to give the population knowledge of what planned interventions will do and to secure real public participation in the decision (paras 236–238). The path to invalidity appears therefore short. A decision approving a project within the Directive’s scope that rests on an assessment omitting significant effects meets, by its very nature, the requirement that the error may have affected the outcome (paras 239–240). The democratic rationale for impact assessment is thus written into the remedy.
As the Court explained, the petroleum operators were not parties to the proceedings, and the declaration of invalidity was therefore not binding on them. Consequently, the approvals did not automatically cease to have effect vis-à-vis the licence holders. Rather, the judgment requires the Ministry to reconsider the approvals in accordance with the applicable environmental assessment requirements, potentially confirming, amending or withdrawing them following a legally compliant procedure.
Democracy and the Separation of Powers Principle
Drawing on its 2020 Peoples v Arctic Oil judgment, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution guarantees environmental rights and access to environmental information. While democratic considerations require judicial restraint in reviewing the political choices underlying environmental decisions, procedural compliance calls for closer scrutiny: the greater a project’s potential consequences, the more rigorous both the environmental assessment and judicial review must be, and the North Sea Fields case concerned procedural errors, rather than the substantive limits of governmental authority (paras 108–111). Writing in the wake of People v Arctic Oil, Minnerop and Røstgaard had already argued that constitutional environmental rights would let courts scrutinise the cumulative effects of global emissions. The Grand Chamber has taken that insight from the field to the shelf.
Who Carries the Risk
The financial stakes are substantial: approximately NOK 21 billion invested in Breidablikk, NOK 7 billion in Tyrving and NOK 177 billion estimated for Yggdrasil (paras 6, 9, 13). Yet the judgment does not decide who would bear the losses if an approval were ultimately revoked. The legal risk was not wholly unforeseeable. US and Australian courts had already addressed combustion emissions (WildEarth Guardians v Zinke and Gloucester Resources v Minister for Planning, both 2019), and Norway’s Supreme Court had indicated in 2020 that global climate effects would be assessed at the PDO stage (paras 4, 7, 10, 155). The Court itself kept the present case alive because it concerned ‘an area under legal development’ of great importance to operators (para 97). Sophisticated licensees could price that risk and arguably should have.
Concluding Remarks
The three Norwegian fields alone are projected to generate close to 400 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent from combustion over their lifetimes (paras 4, 7, 11). This is nine times Norway’s emissions in 2025.
It is worth noting that the global carbon budget will be depleted in less than four years, at current emissions levels, and overshooting 1.5°C is now inevitable. Yet, it remains possible to achieve a ‘lowest possible’ pathway and limit global warming to 1.7–1.8°C before returning to 1.5°C. This allows for a slightly greater budget that future negative emissions may be able to compensate for. EIA can then be considered in relation to scenarios – or their carbon budgets – of the highest possible ambition, the closest to the Paris Agreement objectives.
Just as the ICJ reframed States’ responsibility for climate change in what has been called the Great Reset, the Norwegian Supreme Court’s judgment may mark a reset of its own. The Norwegian reset shows how constitutional procedural rights – as well as interpretation informed by science, regional law and international law – can discipline a (petro-)state’s decisions by amplifying, rather than displacing, democratic choices. Whether more demanding procedure will ultimately change those choices remains open.

a142.texte:
Figures
Abstract
Background
Rising antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens the effectiveness of existing therapies. Ceftriaxone is the only recommended first-line (empiric) treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea in the United States. Ciprofloxacin is no longer recommended for empiric use because of widespread resistance, but it is inexpensive, taken orally, and effective against susceptible infections, which a resistance test can identify. In the context of rising resistance, resistance-guided treatment (RGT) may reduce treatment failures, complications, and inappropriate use of last-line agents while slowing resistance emergence and preserving the efficacy of new and existing drugs. Understanding where RGT provides economic value—across near-term cost savings, delayed resistance emergence, and avoided antibiotic development costs—can illuminate the broader case for investing in resistance testing and help guide pricing and reimbursement decisions.
Methods and findings
We developed an individual-level stochastic simulation model of gonorrhea diagnosis and treatment in the United States, incorporating infection prevalence, symptom status, diagnostic accuracy, resistance profiles, treatment pathways, and partner management (costs in 2025 US dollars[USD]). We evaluated three resistance testing strategies, ciprofloxacin-only, ciprofloxacin + ceftriaxone, and triple-target (including a novel drug A), across a wide range of resistance scenarios. We quantified economic value across three dimensions: (1) per-episode direct medical cost savings, (2) system-level costs attributable to ceftriaxone resistance emergence among men who have sex with men (MSM), and (3) avoided costs of new antibiotic development, estimating the maximum per-test price at which RGT remains cost-neutral. Per-episode cost-neutrality thresholds ranged from near $0 when ceftriaxone resistance was absent to up to $48 per test at 15% prevalence of ceftriaxone resistance (proportion of infections resistant to ceftriaxone). At a prevalence of 50% ciprofloxacin resistance and 5% ceftriaxone resistance, the population-weighted threshold was $7 (95% uncertainty interval [UI] ($3, $11) for a ciprofloxacin-only test and $13 (95% UI [$8–$19]) for a triple-target test. Among MSM, incorporating system-level resistance emergence costs and avoided antibiotic development costs increased the total per-test value to $31 to $114 for a single-target test and $73 to $106 for a triple-target test, depending on whether prescribing practices shift when ceftriaxone resistance reaches 5%. The main limitations are that the model assumes resistance results are available at the same clinical visit to guide initial treatment, does not represent onward transmission or co-resistance between antibiotics, and could estimate longer-term value only for MSM.
Conclusions
Resistance-guided therapy offers economic benefits across multiple dimensions even at relatively high diagnostic prices, supporting investment in gonorrhea resistance testing to improve partner outcomes, delay resistance emergence, and enhance the long-term cost-efficiency of gonorrhea management.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- Rising antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens the effectiveness of ceftriaxone, the only remaining recommended empiric therapy. Preserving new and existing drugs is a public health priority.
- Resistance-guided therapy could reduce treatment failures and complications, improve partner treatment, and slow resistance at the population level, but it is unclear how much such a test could cost and still be worthwhile, or over which time horizons its value accrues.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We built a simulation model of gonorrhea testing and treatment in the United States and estimated the highest price at which a resistance test would still break even against standard care, separately for three kinds of value: savings within the current episode of care, future health-system costs avoided by slowing the rise of ceftriaxone resistance, and avoided costs of developing a new antibiotic.
- Break-even prices within a single episode of care were near zero while ceftriaxone resistance was rare, as it now is in the United States, but rose to $48 per test once 15% of infections were resistant to ceftriaxone. Among men who have sex with men, this break-even price was roughly $31 to $114 per test for a single-target test and $73 to $106 for a triple-target test once the two longer-term kinds of value were included.
- How a test is used mattered as much as what it detects: the triple-target panel had a lower per-test value in some scenarios because its long-term benefit required testing far more people.
What do these findings mean?
- A resistance test for gonorrhea could carry a fairly high price and still save the health system money, particularly once the value of keeping existing antibiotics working is counted alongside the immediate savings from better-targeted treatment.
- Value accrues across several distinct dimensions at once (better outcomes for patients and their partners, delayed emergence of resistance, and deferred spending on new antibiotic development), and separating them gives payers, guideline bodies, and diagnostic developers a framework for pricing, reimbursement, and adoption decisions.
- The main limitations are that we assumed resistance results would be available during the same clinical visit (value fell by over 80% when treatment was given before results returned), did not model how gonorrhea spreads between people, counted only direct medical costs rather than benefits to patients’ health or quality of life, and could estimate longer-term value only for men who have sex with men.

Introduction
Gonorrhea remains a pressing global public health concern, with an estimated 82 million incident cases annually [1]. Rising antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens the effectiveness of ceftriaxone, which is the only remaining recommended empiric therapy [2,3]. The spread of resistant strains has prompted urgent calls for both novel therapeutics and improved diagnostic strategies to guide tailored treatment. Two new antimicrobials, zoliflodacin and gepotidacin, are starting to enter the market [4–6], but preserving their long-term efficacy will be critical to avoid repeating the cycle of rapid resistance emergence that has characterized much of gonorrhea treatment over the past century [7].
Gonorrhea imposes a significant burden on health systems due to its complications. Among women, untreated or inadequately treated infections can result in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), chronic pelvic pain, disseminated gonococcal infection, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal infertility (TI) [8,9]. In men, sequelae such as epididymitis and disseminated gonococcal infection similarly contribute to clinical morbidity and downstream healthcare costs [1,10]. These outcomes carry not only public health consequences but long-term economic consequences for health systems seeking to control sexually transmitted infections.
Resistance-guided treatment (RGT) has been proposed as one strategy to slow the emergence of resistance, preserve the efficacy of both existing and novel therapies, and reduce expenditures associated with treatment failures and complications [11,12]. RGT is already used for other bacterial infections; for example, rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance guides first-line treatment of tuberculosis [13]. This type of approach can also directly improve outcomes for sexual partners by enabling timely and targeted partner treatment. For example, if the index infection is susceptible to ciprofloxacin, a drug that is inexpensive (and less expensive than current partner treatment), widely available, and easily administered, partner treatment can be delivered simply and effectively, often treating two infections at once and preventing onward transmission [14]. Ciprofloxacin was removed from US gonorrhea treatment recommendations in 2007 because of widespread resistance [7], but it remains highly effective against susceptible infections, and molecular assays targeting the gyrA gene can identify such infections at the time of diagnosis [15,16].
Modeling studies indicate that the use of diagnostics to direct antimicrobial selection, particularly in high-incidence populations such as men who have sex with men, may substantially delay the spread of resistant strains and extend the useful life span of current and pipeline drugs [11,17]. In parallel, economic evaluations highlight that, while upfront diagnostic costs are nontrivial, preventing both treatment failures and gonorrhea sequelae can yield significant value over medium- and long-term horizons [18,19]. Moreover, by facilitating appropriate partner treatment and averting persistent infection, resistance testing offers an additional pathway for near-term cost-savings.
Despite this growing body of work, relatively few studies have quantified the economic value of resistance testing across the multiple dimensions relevant to adoption decisions. The value of resistance-guided therapy can be understood at three levels: (1) the near-term budget impact, reflecting direct cost savings from avoided repeat visits, more effective partner management, and fewer complications; (2) the economic value of delaying resistance emergence, which preserves the efficacy of existing low-cost antimicrobials and defers the costs associated with treating resistant infections; and (3) the economic value of avoiding or delaying new antibiotic development, which carries substantial research and development costs ultimately borne across the health system. Importantly, quantifying the value associated with each of these dimensions also enables estimation of the maximum diagnostic price at which resistance testing remains cost-neutral or cost-saving, providing an evidence base for pricing, reimbursement, and adoption decisions.
To address this evidence gap, we developed a simulation model of gonorrhea diagnosis and treatment in the United States that incorporates diagnostic performance, resistance-guided therapy, treatment pathways, partner treatment, and complications. By assigning costs to both immediate clinical management and downstream sequelae, we estimated the per-patient cost of care with and without resistance testing across varying resistance scenarios. Using these estimates, we identified cost-neutral price thresholds for resistance diagnostics, first over short-term clinical decision horizons and then through longer-term impacts of slowing resistance emergence and avoiding new antibiotic development. Specifically, we asked: at what maximum price would gonorrhea resistance testing remain cost-neutral when accounting for savings within a single episode of care, the delayed emergence of ceftriaxone resistance, and avoided new antibiotic development?
Methods
Model overview
We developed an individual-level stochastic simulation model in R (version 4.5.2) to capture the costs and outcomes of gonorrhea treatment under different diagnostic strategies. Each simulated encounter began with a patient presenting to care. The patient was assigned an infection and symptom status, and, if infected, a resistance profile to ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and novel drug A (NDA). Patients then followed one of two diagnostic pathways depending on the scenario: syndromic management, or a same-clinic-visit pathogen identification test followed by reflex resistance testing (with either a single, dual, or triple target test). We assumed pathogen identification must occur during the same encounter, because delayed results would typically lead to empiric treatment for symptomatic patients, limiting the clinical utility of resistance results. We chose an individual-level structure because the costs of interest depend on each patient’s combination of infection, symptom, resistance, test, treatment, and partner outcomes, which are represented more transparently by tracking individuals than by aggregate compartments. Because per-episode costs were estimated at fixed resistance prevalence, the model does not represent transmission; population-level resistance trajectories for the longer-term analyses were instead taken from a previously published transmission model [11].
Diagnostic outcomes were generated probabilistically based on test sensitivity and specificity, and treatment algorithms reflected clinical guidelines, modified when test results indicated resistance (Fig 1: model diagram; Table 1: key model assumptions). Parameter uncertainty is represented by probability distributions (Table 1). If treatment matched the resistance profile, infections were cured; if not, patients risked persistent infection. Those with ongoing symptoms could re-present for care and receive further diagnostic workup, while asymptomatic individuals were less likely to return. We captured only the probability of return due to untreated (or incorrectly treated) gonorrhea, not due to other possible infections requiring follow-up. Partner treatment was modeled probabilistically, conditional on the index case’s results, symptom status, and treatment pathway, with partner infection itself assigned probabilistically rather than assumed. Infected partners shared the index case’s resistance profile, and partners underwent diagnostic testing only if symptomatic after treatment. Resistance to ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and novel drug A was assigned independently for each infection, so co-resistance was not represented. Treatment was assumed to succeed whenever the infection was susceptible to the administered drug, and novel drug B to remain universally effective; the model did not represent failure arising from non-adherence or anatomical site of infection.
The model tracked whether patients achieved cure, remained infected, or developed complications. For women, these included PID and sequelae such as chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and TI; for men, complications included epididymitis and disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), based on U.S. specific estimates [20]. Costs were assigned at each stage, including clinic visits, diagnostics, drugs, and complication management [20]. All analyses were conducted using population-specific gonorrhea prevalence among those tested as a baseline (4.5% for men who have sex with men [MSM], 2.4% for men who have sex with women [MSW], and 1.0% for women) [21,22]. Each scenario (described below) was evaluated using 1,000 probabilistic parameter draws; within each draw, 20,000 individuals were simulated per population group, so that each draw yields a stable estimate of expected cost given that draw’s parameter set. Results are reported as the mean across draws with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs; 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across the 1,000 draws), weighted by sex/population group (MSM, MSW, women).
Resistance testing strategies
We compared three hypothetical resistance testing panels against standard diagnostic management without resistance testing. The underlying rationale differs across approaches: ciprofloxacin-only testing is designed to maximize use of ciprofloxacin whenever possible, since it is inexpensive, orally administered, and easily dispensed to partners. Combination panels that include ceftriaxone and novel drug A (NDA) are additionally aimed at ensuring patients receive the most appropriate therapy when multiple resistance strains are present, thereby preserving last-line and emerging agents.
The specific panels evaluated were:
- CIP-only: testing for ciprofloxacin (CIP) resistance only
- CIP + CRO: testing for ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone (CRO) resistance
- CIP + CRO + NDA: testing for ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and a novel agent A (NDA)
Treatment selection followed observed test results, defaulting to guideline-based empiric therapy when no test was available. If no resistance to ciprofloxacin was detected, ciprofloxacin was used first, followed by ceftriaxone, followed by novel drug A, and finally novel drug B (if resistance to ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and NDA was detected) to which we assume there is no detected resistance across all scenarios.
Model and cost parameterization
To represent real-world care, we included both syndromic management and diagnostic strategies, with and without resistance testing under specified resistance scenarios. The model does not predict how resistance prevalence will evolve; instead, it treats resistance prevalence as an input parameter and estimates the per-episode costs that would result at each specified resistance level. No statistical fitting or model calibration was performed. Parameters for test sensitivity, specificity, treatment efficacy, partner notification, and complication probabilities were drawn from published literature. Table 1 summarizes all key clinical and cost parameters, along with their sources. Further model details and the representation of uncertainty in estimates are described in the S1 Appendix.
Costs were estimated from the Medicaid payer perspective. Immediate management costs (clinic visits, diagnostics, antimicrobials, partner treatment) were derived from US Medicaid fee schedules. Complication costs were sourced from a prior analysis using a broader healthcare perspective (all direct medical costs regardless of payer) [20], which we adjusted to 2025 US dollars. This mixed approach reflects limited availability of Medicaid-specific long-term complication cost data. We estimated direct medical costs across two components: (1) immediate management costs, including clinic visits, diagnostic testing, antimicrobial treatment, partner treatment, and follow-up care for persistent infection; and (2) the expected costs of complications and sequelae attributable to the index episode, including PID, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, TI, epididymitis, and disseminated gonococcal infection. Together, these represent the total expected direct medical cost per clinical episode—that is, the full cost consequences of a single gonorrhea testing encounter, including both near-term management and the downstream medical costs of inadequately treated infection.
Drug costs were based on published and publicly available sources; assumptions were made when data were unavailable. Visit and diagnostic costs were derived from US Medicare fee schedules, with appropriate Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes identified in consultation with providers and billing specialists. This economic evaluation is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) 2022 statement [23] (S1 Appendix).
Estimation of the value of resistance testing by identifying cost-neutral thresholds
We quantified the economic value of resistance testing across three dimensions, each corresponding to a different scope of cost consequence. These dimensions capture non-overlapping categories of cost and are therefore additive: dimension 1 is the direct medical cost saved within the index treatment episode at a fixed resistance level; dimension 2 is the future health-system cost avoided by delaying the rise in ceftriaxone resistance over a 25-year horizon; and dimension 3 is the antibiotic research-and-development cost avoided by preventing that rise. Because each dimension counts a distinct resource, summing them does not double-count. The two variants of dimension 2 (with and without a shift in first-line therapy once resistance reaches 5%) are alternatives and are never added together. For each, we estimated the maximum per-test price at which resistance-guided therapy would remain cost-neutral. Analyses for dimensions 2 and 3 were conducted in Microsoft Excel (version 16.109.3).
1. Per-episode cost-neutrality.
The first dimension captures the value of resistance testing within a single clinical episode. We compared the average per-episode direct medical cost (as defined above) with and without resistance testing across a range of epidemiologic and resistance scenarios. For each population subgroup (MSM, MSW, women), we varied resistance prevalence to ciprofloxacin (10%–70%), ceftriaxone (0%–15%), and novel drug A (0%–5%). For context, the rate of resistance to ciprofloxacin reported by Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP) based on data from across the United States in 2024 (the latest year for which data are available) was 36.9%; for reduced susceptibility to ceftriaxone (the elevated ceftriaxone minimum inhibitory concentration, defined as >0.125 µg/mL) was below 0.1%. These figures were greater among MSM, at 46.7% resistance to ciprofloxacin and 0.3% resistance to ceftriaxone [24]. For each combination, the model estimated the expected per-patient cost with and without resistance testing, where the cost without testing reflects empiric ceftriaxone-based management.

2. System-level cost of resistance emergence.
The second dimension extends the analysis to incorporate the population-level economic consequences of increasing ceftriaxone resistance over time. Because the per-episode cost of gonorrhea care rises with resistance prevalence (due to higher rates of treatment failure, repeat visits, and complications), delaying resistance emergence has direct economic value.
We estimated this value over a 25-year time horizon. First, we compared the total system cost in a scenario with 0% ceftriaxone resistance to one with 5% ceftriaxone resistance, reflecting the incremental cost attributable to that change (holding ciprofloxacin resistance at 50% and NDA resistance at 0%). We then multiplied the annual number of MSM presenting for gonorrhea testing by the per-episode cost under each resistance scenario and summed over 25 years, discounting future costs at 3% annually. The difference between these two totals represents the aggregate cost attributable to a 5 percentage-point increase in ceftriaxone resistance.
We used previously published transmission modeling of the gonorrhea epidemic among MSM in the United States to estimate the extent to which resistance testing could delay reaching 5% ceftriaxone resistance [11]. From that work, testing 10% of MSM diagnosed with gonorrhea using a single-target resistance test could delay reaching 5% resistance by 5 years, and testing 50% of MSM diagnosed with gonorrhea using a triple-target resistance test could prevent the emergence of ceftriaxone resistance over the entire modeled period. For the single-target test, we assumed a linear increase from 0% to 5% ceftriaxone resistance over 15 years, followed by continued linear increase thereafter. For the triple-target test, we assumed resistance remains at 0% for the full 25-year horizon. To translate these system-level savings into a per-test value, we divided the total cost attributable to resistance emergence by the total number of resistance tests required over the relevant time horizon.
Finally, we repeated this analysis under an alternative scenario in which, once ceftriaxone resistance reaches 5%, first-line empiric therapy shifts to NDA ($50 per course). This scenario captures a larger cost differential, because the more expensive replacement drug amplifies the per-episode cost consequences of resistance. Given that the underlying transmission modeling is available only for MSM in the United States, these system-level analyses could not be extended to other populations.
3. Economic value of avoiding new antibiotic development.
The third dimension estimates the economic value of resistance testing in delaying or avoiding the need to develop a new antibiotic for gonorrhea. We assumed a development cost of approximately $1.2 billion per new antibiotic [25], that the United States represents 44% of the global market for antibiotics [26], and that the proportion of gonorrhea treatment in the United States that occurs among MSM (S1 Appendix, 52%). The development cost attributable to gonorrhea treatment among MSM in the United States is therefore $1.2 billion × 44% × 52% = $275 million.
Using the resistance trajectory estimates described above, we calculated the total number of triple-target resistance tests required to prevent the emergence of resistance over a 25-year time horizon. The per-test value of avoiding new antibiotic development was then estimated by dividing the attributable development cost ($275 million) by the total number of tests required.
This analysis applies only to the triple-target test, as only this strategy was projected to fully prevent resistance emergence in the underlying transmission model [11].
Uncertainty analysis
Given the wide number of scenarios evaluated and the probabilistic nature of the model, additional uncertainty analysis was limited to deterministic sensitivity analysis by key additional uncertain parameters. This included determining how changing the specific partner-notification rate affected threshold cost (20%–50%), the probability of the partner of the index client being truly infected (30%–65%), the cost of novel drugs A and B (varying from $25 to $500, as future prices are uncertain), probability of returning to care with symptoms (70%–95%), and resistance test performance (resistance-detection sensitivity 92%–100%; specificity 96%–100%). Parameter uncertainty was quantified through the probabilistic sensitivity analysis (Table 1) and the one-way deterministic sensitivity analysis (S1 Appendix).

Results
Baseline costs without resistance testing
We first estimated the average per-person cost of care for individuals diagnosed with gonorrhea under standard practice (without resistance testing). At 50% ciprofloxacin resistance, 0% ceftriaxone resistance, and 0% NDA resistance, the mean per-person cost of care was $331 (95% UI [$311, $360] for MSM, $508 (95% UI [$375, $726]) for MSW, and $869 (95% UI [$706, $1,104]) for women, a weighted average of $508 (95% UI [$427,$630]) (Fig 2). The higher costs for MSW mainly reflect complications among their female partners, while higher costs for women are driven by more extensive diagnostic workup and greater complication costs. Increasing ceftriaxone resistance increased the average cost of care due to higher rates of incorrect empiric treatment and downstream clinical management; when ceftriaxone resistance increases to 5%, the cost per person with gonorrhea who is tested increases in MSM to $343 (95% UI [$322, $373]), in MSW to $529 (95% UI [$392,$744]) and in women to $903 (95% UI [$741, $1,145]), with a weighted average of $528 (95% UI [$446, $652]) per person diagnosed with gonorrhea. This 5% increase in ceftriaxone resistance alone results in an increase in the total cost of gonorrhea care by 3.9% from $485 million/year to $504 million/year in the United States, when multiplying the annual number of diagnosed and treated cases (S1 Appendix) by the cost per case. Assuming no shift in first-line antibiotics with an increase in ceftriaxone resistance, a 15% prevalence of ceftriaxone resistance would cost $536 million annually for gonorrhea-related care in the U.S., a 10.3% increase in total costs.
For people diagnosed with gonorrhea, in all scenarios, the cost per person with gonorrhea is largely driven by the initial visit cost (49% of total cost for MSM, 32% for MSW, and 19% for women) and initial diagnostic workup cost (39% of total cost for MSM, 25% for MSW, and 48% for women). The remaining cost is almost entirely complications for the index client and their partners (9% of total cost for MSM, 41% for MSW, and 31% for women) (Fig 3). When ceftriaxone resistance is absent, resistance testing offers no savings because empiric ceftriaxone therapy is already effective for all patients. However, once ceftriaxone resistance reaches approximately 2.5% or higher, the introduction of a CIP-only or CIP + CRO resistance test reduces total per-episode costs relative to standard care. This is because higher resistance prevalence increases the probability of empiric treatment failure, which in turn increases costs from follow-up visits, repeat diagnostics, and complications—costs that resistance-guided therapy can avoid.
Estimation of the value of resistance testing by identifying cost-neutral thresholds
Short-term cost neutrality estimation.
Rising prevalence of ciprofloxacin resistance decreased the cost-neutral threshold for all three resistance testing panels (CIP-only, CIP + CRO, and CIP + CRO + NDA), because fewer patients had ciprofloxacin-susceptible infections, reducing the opportunity to replace ceftriaxone with a lower-cost oral alternative (Fig 4). In other words, the value of a resistance test that identifies ciprofloxacin susceptibility diminishes as the proportion of patients who could benefit from that result shrinks, illustrating that the economic value of a resistance test is inherently linked to the availability and cost of the treatment it enables. Conversely, increasing ceftriaxone resistance raised the per-test cost-neutral price from near $0 (and in some instances <$0, when ceftriaxone resistance was 0%) to as high as $48 per test when ceftriaxone resistance reached 15%. This occurred because higher ceftriaxone resistance increased the probability of empiric treatment failure under standard care, which in turn increased costs from repeat visits, diagnostic workup, partner care, and complications.
Across scenarios, cost-neutrality thresholds for resistance tests varied widely, and estimates were also subject to stochastic variability. At 50% ciprofloxacin resistance, 5% ceftriaxone resistance, and 0% novel drug A resistance, the population-weighted cost-neutral price per CIP-only resistance test was $7 (95% UI [$3, $11]), and $13 (95% UI [$8, $19]) for a triple-target (CIP + CRO + NDA) test. If the resistance rate to novel drug A is also 5%, then the population-weighted cost-neutral price for both resistance tests remained the same as with 0% novel drug A resistance. S1 Appendix describes the results of the deterministic sensitivity analysis.
System-level cost of resistance emergence (MSM only)
Separately from the per-episode analysis above, we estimated the additional per-test value of using resistance testing to delay increases in ceftriaxone resistance over a 25-year time horizon. This value captures system-level costs that resistance testing could help avoid and is additive to the per-episode cost-neutrality thresholds reported above. These longer-term analyses were restricted to MSM because the published transmission model used to project the effect of resistance testing on ceftriaxone resistance is available only for MSM in the United States [11], and because MSM account for the majority of US gonorrhea diagnoses (S1 Appendix) and have a higher prevalence of resistance than other groups [24].
Under a scenario in which prescribing practices do not change when ceftriaxone resistance emerges, the additional per-test value of delaying resistance is $25 (95% UI [$19, $28]) for a CIP-only test and $19 (95% UI [$14, $21]) for a triple-target test. If instead first-line therapy transitions to a new antibiotic (assumed cost of $50/course) once ceftriaxone resistance reaches 5%, the additional per-test value increases to $108 (95% UI [$58, $141]) for a CIP-only test (applied to 10% of diagnosed cases) and $52 (95% UI [$33, $63]) for a triple-target test (applied to 50% of diagnosed cases).

La procédure simplifiée est, depuis 2022, une procédure de sanction de la CNIL adaptée aux dossiers ne présentant pas de difficulté juridique particulière. Contrairement à la procédure « ordinaire », le président de la (ou un de ses membres) décide seul de la sanction. Une sanction simplifiée ne peut pas excéder 20 000 € et la CNIL ne peut pas divulguer le nom de l’organisme sanctionné. Grâce à cette procédure, la CNIL agit ainsi plus rapidement pour sanctionner les organismes afin de protéger les droits des personnes concernées.
Depuis juin 2026, la CNIL a prononcé 38 nouvelles sanctions dans le cadre de sa procédure simplifiée, pour un montant cumulé d’amendes de 302 800 euros. Ces décisions portent principalement sur les cookies, la sécurité des données, la prospection commerciale et la non coopération avec la CNIL. Cela porte à 61 le nombre de sanctions simplifiées prononcées depuis début 2026.
Des manquements aux règles relatives aux cookies
À la suite de contrôles en ligne de plusieurs sites web (société d’édition, sociétés proposant la vente de vêtements ou de véhicules, etc.), la CNIL a constaté que les bandeaux d’information relatifs aux cookies ne comprenaient pas une information complète (défaut d’information sur les finalités des cookies, le et la manière de refuser ou de retirer son consentement).
Elle a également constaté que des cookies étaient déposés sans consentement et avant toute action de la part de l’utilisateur, ou après son refus, alors que ces cookies ne relèvent pas de l’exemption de consentement prévue à l’article 82 de la loi Informatique et Libertés (c’est le cas, par exemple, des cookies publicitaires).
Ces investigations ont abouti une douzaine d’amendes.
Des manquements à la sécurité des données
La CNIL a également sanctionné une douzaine d’organismes pour des manquements à la sécurité des données à caractère personnel, en raison de différents défauts de sécurité.
Les mots de passe étaient insuffisamment robustes, c’est-à-dire qu’ils ne comportaient pas de règle de complexité suffisante (par exemple, un mot de passe pouvait être composé d’un seul caractère). Ceci peut conduire à des attaques par des tiers non autorisés, telles que des attaques par « force brute » ou « par dictionnaire », qui consistent à tester successivement et de façon systématique de nombreux mots de passe et conduisent ainsi à une compromission des comptes associés et des données personnelles qu’ils contiennent.
L’accès à la base de données des clients se faisait par des comptes génériques partagés par plusieurs personnes. Or, l’une des précautions indispensables pour assurer la traçabilité des accès est de définir un identifiant unique par utilisateur, grâce à des comptes individuels, permettant d’identifier les accès illégitimes.
Les fonctions de n’étaient pas conformes à l’état de l’art, comme la fonction SHA-1 qui ne permet pas de prévenir les vulnérabilités et facilite le décryptage des données chiffrées, par des acteurs malveillants.
Des manquements relatifs à la prospection commerciale
La CNIL a sanctionné 6 organismes pour des manquements relatifs à la prospection commerciale.
Des organismes ont transmis des données personnelles à des partenaires pour réaliser de la prospection commerciale électronique, ou ont eux-mêmes réalisé des opérations de prospection commerciale à partir de données collectées par le biais de formulaires de jeux-concours, sans disposer d’un consentement valable pour ces opérations.
La conception des formulaires de collecte incitait les personnes à consentir à la transmission de leurs données à des fins de prospection commerciale. La conception des formulaires mettait particulièrement en valeur l’option consistant à accepter de recevoir des offres promotionnelles, laissant croire qu’il s’agissait du seul moyen de valider la participation au jeu-concours. Les personnes n’étaient donc pas mesure de consentir de manière libre et univoque à l’utilisation de leurs données en matière de prospection commerciale.
Défaut de coopération avec la CNIL
6 organismes ont été sanctionnés pour un défaut de coopération avec la CNIL.
Des organismes n’ont pas répondu à des demandes de la CNIL sollicitant des précisions sur la mise en place de dispositif vidéo ou sur des demandes de droit d’accès ou d’effacement, ce qui a conduit la CNIL à prononcer une amende à leur encontre.
Pour rappel, la coopération avec la CNIL est une obligation légale (article 18 de la loi Informatique et Libertés).

EU Sanctions Irish Journalist Over Russian Disinformation WSJ

SOURCE 2 (RTE.ie) :
Irish journalist Chay Bowes has been sanctioned by the EU as an alleged propagandist for the Russian government.
The listing was announced by EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels.
In a statement, member states said that Mr Bowes, who works for the Russian media outlet RT, had "participated in information manipulation and dissemination of narratives that legitimise and sustain the ongoing Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine."
He was one of 113 people and entities listed by EU foreign ministers in connection with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Member states listed Russian television figures Vitaly Eliseev and Petr Marchenko, as well as Ukrainian-born blogger and military commentator Yurii Podoliaka alongside Mr Bowes.
Mr Bowes, who describes himself on his Instagram profile as an "Irish journalist, writer, broadcaster and troublemaker", is a former shareholder in, and founding member of, Irish news website The Ditch.
He was invited by Russia to address the UN Security Council by video link in 2023, when he blamed the war on NATO, describing a "frenzied, incalculable, loosely regulated" flood of weapons into Ukraine.
He was introduced at the UN as a "scholar specialising in small arms and munitions".
He said that NATO planners and an "ever-hawkish Anglosphere" were driving the "seemingly perpetual escalation of military aid to Ukraine".
His comments were condemned by Ukraine's ambassador to the UN at the time.
In a legal text, 45-year-old Mr Bowes is described as "an Irish citizen working as a correspondent for the Russian transnational influence channel RT International."
The text says he has been the host of an RT show called 'Moscow Mules' since February 2024 and that he co-founded a pro-Russian disinformation network called The Islander News.
It states: "Bowes is involved in numerous information operations conducted by the Foundation to Battle Injustice (R-FBI), which was created by the Wagner Group and listed by the [European] Union on July 2025."
The text says Bowes is also involved in "the regular amplification of content produced by the Russian Information Manipulation Set (IMS) Storm-1516."
The text concluded that Bowes was "implementing, supporting and facilitating actions or policies attributable to the Government of the Russian Federation which undermine or threaten democracy, the rule of law, stability or security in the Union, in an international organisation and in third countries, by planning, directing, engaging in, directly or indirectly, supporting or otherwise facilitating the use of coordinated information manipulation and interference."
Mr Bowes said in a social media post that "the authoritarian EU sanctioned me, no recourse to defend myself, no hearing, no evidence" and insisted that "Their allegations against me are utterly baseless".
He added: "They want to bully me into silence, they want to deny you your God-given right to hear dissenting opinions, they want to kill freedom of speech."
People Before Profit leader Richard Boyd Barrett, also writing on social media, called the sanction "A sinister move seriously threatening free speech and press".
"RT is a mouthpiece for Russian state that never criticises Putin but we have lots of voices on western media who push NATO, EU, US, Israeli propaganda with no sanction," he said.
The EU also listed 24 individuals connected to Russia’s Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based public relations company, which, according to a statement, "carries out large scale information manipulation and interference projects funded, directed and supervised by the Russian Presidential Administration."
Foreign ministers said the SDA "systematically manipulates the media and social media environment, spreads pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation and foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns".
The listings also include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions.
Speaking on her arrival at a monthly EU foreign ministers meeting this morning, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said the listings came ahead of further discussions this week on a broader 22nd sanctions package on Russia.
Watch: Helen McEntee says EU has agreed on sanctions against 133 people, entities
Ukraine's financial, humanitarian needs assessed
EU foreign ministers are meeting to assess Ukraine's financial and humanitarian needs as Russia continues to destroy the country’s energy and water infrastructure.
The meeting comes in the wake of Friday’s informal EU summit in Dublin, at which EU leaders agreed the format for Europe’s involvement in potential peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, brokered by the United States.
Ministers will discuss ways of getting Ukraine the air defence systems it needs to counter Russia’s escalating waves of ballistic missile and jet-powered drone strikes.
Russia is continuing to strike Ukraine’s energy and water infrastructure, causing misery for millions of civilians, while also hitting the country’s grain exports in the Black Sea, a vital source of income.
Ministers will hear from their Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on the country’s needs as winter tightens its grip.
On Wednesday, the European Commission will come forward with a proposal on how to tackle Ukraine’s €70 billion funding gap next year, while on Thursday the so-called Coalition of the Willing will meet in Berlin.
That is the ad hoc group of some 36 countries, led by the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, which could provide a peace keeping or peace enforcement mission in Ukraine should a ceasefire take effect.
Ms McEntee welcomed the prospect of Europe being present at negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, and the agreement in Dublin on Friday among EU leaders as to the structure of the European negotiating team.
She said: "I think naturally there will be a question as to how this works next. Importantly, it was agreed that Europe, firstly, would be around the table. That has not been the case until recently.
"It's really important now that we have a structure beyond that to make sure that any meetings that happen, that we have an agreed mandate, that we have an agreed position, that we focus on not just the security environment, because I think we tend to focus just on the security environment post a ceasefire.
"We need to look at politically where Europe needs to be involved. You need to look at economically where Europe needs to be involved from a humanitarian situation. What more we can do while also then focusing on the security aspect of it."
She added: "In the wake of all of this positive momentum, Russia has clearly not changed its position. It is continuing its attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure."

Ceasefire needed before peace talks, says Kallas
Earlier, EU foreign police chief Kaja Kallas said that Europe will need to see concessions from Russia and a ceasefire in Ukraine before serious peace talks could begin.
She also stressed the need for Europe to concentrate on the substance of any possible peace agreement and have a reply to Russia's "maximum demands".
France and Britain will hold a conference on 4 December on tackling Russia's "shadow fleet", France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
"I will host in Paris on December 4, at the request of the President of the Republic, an international conference dedicated to the fight against the Russian shadow fleet," Mr Barrot told reporters at the meeting in Brussels.
Sanctions on Russia for invading Ukraine and aimed at cutting its oil revenue have spawned a fleet of often ageing and unregulated vessels helping Moscow keep its crude exports flowing.
EU naval forces last week boarded a suspected Russian shadow fleet crude tanker in the Mediterranean, Ms Kallas said yesterday.
Increasing danger of nuclear accident flagged
The risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine is increasing this winter, nuclear safety regulators representing 38 countries has said, urging Russia to stop its attacks on the country's power infrastructure.
Moscow has stepped up its drone and missile attacks on Ukrainian energy installations, such as plants, power lines and electricity substations, a system already weakened after nearly five years of conflict.
"Together we... express our deep concern about the increasing risks to nuclear safety arising from Russia's war against Ukraine, and its continued attacks on the country's energy infrastructure," the bodies said in a joint statement seen by Reuters ahead of publication.
"Together, (we) see an urgent need for Russia to cease attacks against Ukraine's nuclear facilities and the energy infrastructure essential to their safe operation."
The regulators' key concern is that, without a stable electricity supply from the grid, it becomes more and more difficult for Ukrainian nuclear plants to keep their nuclear material cool and avoid a meltdown.
If that were to occur, there could be releases of radioactivity into the air as happened during the 1986 Chornobyl disaster, considered to be the world's worst civil nuclear accident.
Ukraine hits key Crimean bridge
Ukraine fired hundreds of drones at Russia overnight, aiming towards Moscow and hitting a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia.
The strike on the bridge appeared to inflict only minor damage, though it drew an angry response from the Kremlin.
Ukraine launched 1,336 drones in the barrage, Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement, the second-highest daily figure so far this year, according to an AFP tally of official Russian statements.
The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. US officials say Russia's war against Ukraine is not expected to be a focus of the talks.
"The enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," Crimea's Russian-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov wrote on Telegram.
He did not say whether anyone was killed or wounded in the strike.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later told reporters that there was "minor damage" and that traffic was continuing.
He also issued a rare admission of vulnerability in Russia's air defence system.
"Unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100 percent protection against such large-scale strikes on various targets," he said.
The bridge has been a key target for Ukraine since Russia launched its offensive in February 2022.
It has been struck several times, including an October 2022 blast in which an explosive-packed truck was detonated on the bridge, causing months of disruption.
Around 600 of the drones were intercepted on approach to the Russian capital, Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site.
Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Moscow's own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid -- attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions.
Russia says Estonian border closures will backfire
Moscow has denied being behind sabotage attacks that prompted Estonia to close its border with Russia, implying the decision would only backfire on Tallinn.
Estonia announced Sunday it was closing border checkpoints with its ex-Soviet neighbour after saying it had thwarted an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.
"These statements have no basis whatsoever ... no evidence, nothing," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday.
"They are absolutely unfounded and we cannot take such accusations seriously," he added, referring to what he called "similar accusations" from other European countries.
Several countries across the EU have accused Russia of being behind sabotage attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine, in what many see as a rise of so-called "hybrid warfare."
Tallinn said the borders would close on December 1.
"Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls," Peskov said.
Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, currently has three crossing points with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, that allow the movement of people and goods between the two countries.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to pass.
The crossings are among the few remaining overland links between Russia and the European Union still operating since Moscow launched its full-scale offensive on Ukraine in February 2022.
Irish diplomat steps down as envoy
David O'Sullivan, a former senior Irish civil servant at EU level, has confirmed he is stepping down as the EU's Russia sanctions envoy.
In a brief statement to RTÉ News, Mr O'Sullivan said: "I'm stepping down because I've done four years and I think it’s time for somebody new to take over."
Mr O’Sullivan was appointed by the European Commission as International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions in December 2022, tasked with ensuring that third countries complied with sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.
He has spent the past four years meeting governments across the globe to press against circumvention of sanctions, with Russia frequently finding ways to evade export controls.
Before taking up the role, Mr O’Sullivan was Director-General of the Institute of International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin and had served as EU ambassador to the United States.
He was the chief operating officer of the EU’s diplomatic arm, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and had been secretary general of the European Commission between 2005-2010.
Mr O’Sullivan has commented on the government’s response to the allegations surrounding Aughinish Alumina’s exports of alumina to Russia.
At an IIEA meeting in October, Mr O’Sullivan said he had "no doubt the investigative journalists got it right", adding that: "The alumina goes to smelters in Russia, who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex."
It’s understood the European Commission is seeking a replacement for Mr O’Sullivan to take up the sanctions envoy role.
Additional reporting: AFP, Reuters

L’ESSENTIEL
- Un nouveau compartiment constitué d’ARN et de protéines a été découvert par Noemi Zollo, alors étudiante en thèse, dans les petits ovocytes de souris.
- Il a fallu un long travail collectif pour passer des premières observations à la description de ce qui sera appelé « le corps de Zollo » (Zollo Body).
- Découvrez cette histoire scientifique, mais surtout humaine, qui pourrait avoir des implications sur la question de la fertilité des femmes.
Nous sommes issus de la fusion entre un gros ovule et un petit spermatozoïde. L’ovule se forme à partir d’une cellule qu’on appelle l’ovocyte, qui a grossi dans l’ovaire de notre maman, puis en a été expulsé pour rencontrer un spermatozoïde. Mais comment l’ovocyte grossit-il ? C’est là que notre histoire commence. Par la découverte d’une nouvelle structure, un compartiment intracellulaire, au cœur du processus de la croissance en taille de l’ovocyte.
Comme la plupart des découvertes, c’est une histoire de hasard, de contexte, de persévérance et de rencontres scientifiques. Elle démarre par la curiosité d’une étudiante en thèse, Noemi Zollo (l’une des autrices de cet article), observant un amas d’ARN collé au noyau des petits ovocytes de souris, mais pas dans les gros. Comment des ARN peuvent-ils rester ensemble regroupés en un amas ? Des découvertes récentes ont montré que c’était possible grâce à la formation de structures particulières, comprenant ARN et protéines associées aux ARN, qui, ensemble, forment des condensats.
De nombreux condensats ont été caractérisés, avec des fonctions variées allant du contrôle de la transcription de l’ADN, à la modification et au stockage des ARN. Dans l’équipe, nous avions même découvert, peu de temps auparavant, que les forces du cytosquelette (structures intracellulaires qui font bouger les compartiments) influençaient l’architecture et l’activité de certains types de condensats.
Parmi ces condensats, le corps de Balbiani, dont les premières descriptions remontent au XIXᵉ siècle, est observé dans les ovocytes de vertébrés au tout début de leur formation dans les ovaires, lorsqu’ils sont encore dormants (un ovocyte qui n’a pas été stimulé hormonalement pour croître et donc qui reste dans l’ovaire). Ce corps de Balbiani est un supercondensat, puisqu’il contient non seulement des ARN et leurs protéines associées, mais aussi de nombreux organites. Sa fonction est le stockage et la préservation des organites qui le constituent. Il est, lui aussi, collé au noyau des ovocytes dormants.
Une découverte, fruit de nombreuses rencontres
L’amas d’ARN observé grâce à une sonde fluorescence, par Noemi, lors des étapes de formation d’un ovocyte, contient lui aussi de nombreux organites, mitochondries (production de l’énergie cellulaire), Golgi (modification et tri des protéines et lipides), réticulum endoplasmique (fabrique des protéines et lipides), lysosomes (digestion et recyclage des déchets). Quelle est donc cette structure que nous nommons le « corps de Zollo », du nom de famille de Noemi qui l’a observé la première ?
Quelle est sa composition ? Comment la caractériser ? Quelles sont ses fonctions ? Ces trois questions seront les lignes directrices de la thèse de Noemi. Au hasard d’une invitation à un séminaire scientifique, nous rencontrons Gabriele Zaffagnini et Elvan Böke à Barcelone. Gabriele, dans le laboratoire d’Elvan, était justement en train de caractériser un autre supercondensat constitué lui aussi d’organites, présent dans l’ovocyte après la phase de croissance, dont la fonction est la dégradation de protéines non fonctionnelles. Une sorte d’usine de nettoyage de la cellule permettant à l’ovocyte d’éliminer « ses déchets » juste avant sa rencontre avec le spermatozoïde et sa transformation en un embryon.
Le travail de Gabriele et d’Elvan nous inspire et nous pousse à isoler le Zollo Body en « déchirant » mécaniquement les ovocytes afin de pouvoir en étudier sa composition en ARN et protéines. Ce tour de force technique en raison de la rareté du matériel expérimental (30 ovocytes au stade Zollo Body par souris) et de la difficulté à « déchirer » un ovocyte à l’aide d’une pipette très fine sans la boucher, rendu possible grâce au talent de dissection de Noemi, a été décisif dans l’étude de cette structure.
La collecte minutieuse de dizaines de corps de Zollo et d’ovocytes entiers est donc réalisée et envoyée à Barcelone pour analyse des protéines par Gabriele et Elvan. Gabriele récupère les échantillons congelés, les traite avec des enzymes qui vont digérer les protéines de nos échantillons en petits peptides qui seront séquencés. L’analyse de ces séquences de peptides sera effectuée pour une identification et une quantification des protéines murines correspondantes. Ainsi, nous aurons une idée plus précise des protéines plus concentrées dans le corps de Zollo par rapport à celles présentes dans la totalité de l’ovocyte.
Cette analyse a permis de confirmer l’enrichissement en mitochondries, Golgi et réticulum endoplasmique, observé par immunofluorescence et par microscopie in vivo. L’enrichissement en protéines ribosomales et protéines de la machinerie de synthèse des protéines nous a aussi mis la puce à l’oreille vers une fonction inédite de synthèse des protéines.
Comment démontrer le rôle du corps de Zollo ?
Nous nous donc sommes concentrés sur cette fonction et nous avons mis en évidence, par plusieurs techniques complémentaires, la présence d’une traduction locale des protéines au sein du corps de Zollo. Nous avons aussi montré indirectement que la quantité totale de protéines augmentait très significativement, accompagnant l’augmentation brutale de la taille des ovocytes à la fin de leur croissance. Ce résultat étant important, car plusieurs études précédentes avaient établi que des cellules forcées à grossir de façon non physiologique voyaient leur cytoplasme se diluer en concentration de protéines et, ainsi, leur viabilité chuter. Les ovocytes étaient donc capables de grossir rapidement de manière naturelle sans diluer leur concentration protéique du cytoplasme, préservant leur viabilité.
Mais comment démontrer l’importance de cette structure dans la physiologie de l’ovocyte ? Là encore, le hasard et le contexte. Dans le laboratoire de Melina Schuh (Institut Max-Planck, Göttingen), en Allemagne, Christopher Thomas (co-auteur de cet article) avait mis au point un système révolutionnaire permettant de suivre en direct le processus d’ovulation en dehors du corps de l’animal. Ses films montrant un ovocyte au sein de sa niche (ou follicule ovarien) se transformer en un ovule étaient spectaculaires.
Nous l’avons invité à donner un séminaire au Centre interdisciplinaire de recherche en biologie (CIRB) du Collège de France. Christopher, qui démarrait son équipe à l’Institut de biologie du développement de Marseille (IBDM), nous a dit qu’il était aussi capable de mettre au point un système d’imagerie de la croissance folliculaire en dehors de la souris. Il n’en fallait pas plus pour démarrer une collaboration avec lui ! Christopher a mis au point ce système de suivi par microscopie optique de la croissance folliculaire in vitro. En utilisant les bons marqueurs mitochondriaux, que Noemi avait testés auparavant, il a pu voir précisément le moment de formation du corps de Zollo dans l’ovocyte au sein de sa niche de cellules folliculaires.
Alors que Noemi avait fait toutes ses expériences sur des ovocytes isolés de leur niche de cellules folliculaires, les observations de Christopher démontraient que le corps de Zollo se formait bien de manière physiologique dans l’ovocyte entouré de ses cellules folliculaires. Christopher a été plus loin, ayant en main un système de croissance ovocytaire et folliculaire (les deux allant de pair), il a testé des inhibiteurs de la synthèse des protéines sur son modèle expérimental. Sans succès. Sa curiosité a été attirée ensuite vers des inhibiteurs préalablement caractérisés de protéines de la même famille présentes dans le Zollo Body et identifiées par notre spectrométrie de masse, DDX3X et DDX5. Et là, bingo !
L’inhibiteur de DDX5 induisait en quelques heures la dissolution du corps de Zollo ainsi que l’arrêt de la croissance ovocytaire et folliculaire. Noemi a confirmé l’effet de cet inhibiteur sur le corps de Zollo sur des ovocytes isolés. Nous avons ainsi pu proposer au moins une fonction à ce corps de Zollo : permettre la synthèse efficace des protéines dans les ovocytes afin de favoriser une croissance en taille, qui s’accélère en fin d’ovogenèse, tout en évitant la dilution du cytoplasme.
Ainsi corps de Balbiani et corps de Zollo se ressemblent dans leur architecture, mais ils présentent des fonctions divergentes, l’un associé à la dormance et à la protection des ARN des ovocytes en tout début d’ovogenèse, l’autre associé à un haut métabolisme, à une croissance rapide et à une synthèse protéique à partir de ARN en fin d’ovogenèse.
Un lien avec la fertilité des femmes ?
Il reste de nombreuses questions ouvertes : est-ce important pour la cellule de rassembler les organites dans une telle structure ? Est-ce pour augmenter l’efficacité de synthèse et de sécrétion de protéines dans une cellule déjà énorme au départ ? ou est-ce que ce condensat a d’autres fonctions ? De manière intéressante le corps de Zollo grandit proportionnellement à la croissance de l’ovocyte : petit dans les petits ovocytes et gros dans les plus gros. Ce corps sert-il de mètre étalon, permettant de former des organites, mitochondries, Golgi, réticulum endoplasmique, lysosomes de manière proportionnelle et adaptée à la taille de l’ovocyte afin que sa densité cytoplasmique reste constante ? Et, si oui, comment peut-il effectuer une telle fonction ? Quelles sont les boucles de rétrocontrôles mises en place ?
Enfin, Elsa Labrune, des Hospices civils de Lyon, a pu détecter une structure qui ressemblerait au corps de Zollo dans les ovocytes humains. Est-ce bien la même structure ? Possède-t-elle aussi une fonction d’accompagnement de la croissance dans les ovocytes humains ? Ces questions sont extrêmement importantes dans le contexte de la préservation de fertilité.
En effet, nous avons montré que le corps de Zollo de l’ovocyte de souris était dissous par des drogues impactant les microtubules, éléments du cytosquelette cellulaire. Or, les taxanes, qui impactent les microtubules, sont très souvent utilisés en chimiothérapie. Ils pourraient potentiellement affecter le corps de Zollo des ovocytes humains et ainsi abîmer le stock d’ovocytes en croissance.
Il est donc essentiel que les femmes n’ayant pas encore eu d’enfant et étant traitées par chimiothérapie pour un cancer soient informées grâce à une consultation d’oncofertilité des options de préservation de leurs ovules avant les traitements, ce qui ne semble pas encore fait de manière systématique.
